title: U.S. Coast Guard Academy Boards Packet 2026–2027
scope: Content through CHAPTER 2 APPEARANCE AND GROOMING. REFERENCES and all material after this chapter are intentionally omitted.
note: This is a reorganization of the packet content, not a determination of what is or is not board-required. Source wording is retained as closely as possible.

academy_mission.section: The Mission of the United States Coast Guard Academy

items.title: Mission
items.meaning: The mission of the United States Coast Guard Academy is to graduate young men and women with sound bodies, stout hearts, and alert minds, with a liking for the sea and its lore, and with that high sense of honor, loyalty, and obedience which goes with trained initiative and leadership; well-grounded in seamanship, the sciences, and the amenities, andstrong in the resolve to be worthy of the traditions of commissioned officers in the United States Coast Guard in the service of their country and humanity.

items.title: Origin
items.meaning: Composed in 1929 by VADM Harry G. Hamlet while Superintendent of the Academy

items.phrase: In Service to our Nation. With Honor, Respect, and Devotion to Duty We protect. We defend. We save. We are Semper Paratus. We are the United States Coast Guard.

items.order: To take charge of this post and all government property in view.
To walk my post in a military manner, keeping always on the alert and observing everything that takes place within sight or hearing.
To report all violations of orders I am instructed to enforce.
To repeat all calls from posts more distant from the guardhouse than my own.
To quit my post only when properly relieved.
To receive, obey, and pass on to the sentry who relieves me all orders from the commanding officer, officer of the day, and officers and petty officers of the watch.
To talk to no one except in the line of duty.
To give the alarm in case of fire or disorder.
To call the officer of the deck in any case not covered by instructions.
To salute all officers and all colors and standards not cased.
To be especially watchful at night, and during the time for challenging, to challenge all persons on or near my post and to allow no one to pass without the proper authority.

items.action: Apply the ordered rudder. Standard rudder is the amount required to turn the ship on its standard tactical diameter, normally 20 degrees. Full rudder is the amount required to steer on a reduced tactical diameter, normally 30 degrees. The rudder angle can vary from ship to ship.

Apply the ordered rudder. The Conn can follow this order with a new course for the Helmsman to steer, such as “STEADY ON COURSE 256” or another rudder command. If the Conn does not specify a course, the Helmsmen must call out the heading at 10-degree increments, such as “PASSING TO THE RIGHT 150, PASSING TO THE RIGHT 160” until the Conn orders a course.

items.command:
EASE YOUR RUDDER

EASE YOUR RUDDER TO RIGHT/LEFT ## DEGREES
items.action: Decrease the rudder angle by half the amount currently applied or by the amount ordered. The Conn can follow this order with a new course for the Helmsman to steer or another rudder command. If the Conn does not specify a course, the Helmsman must call out the heading at 10-degree increments until the Conn orders a course.
Place the rudder at zero degrees.
Use the rudder as necessary to check the swing of the ship without steadying on any specific course.

items.command:
STEADY
STEADY AS SHE GOES
STEADY ON COURSE ###
items.action: Steer the course on which the ship is currently headed or the ordered course. If the ship is turning and the Conn gives the command STEADY or STEADY AS SHE GOES, the Helmsman notes the heading and responds “MARK, ###,” calling the heading of the ship at that point. The Helmsman then steers the ship to that heading and calls “STEADY ON COURSE ###,” when the heading has been reached.
The Helmsman steers on a range or object identified by the Conning Officer.
Move the rudder to the same angle in the opposite direction from where it is currently ordered. The Conn can only give this order when a specific rudder angle is in effect.

items.command: NOTHING TO THE RIGHT/LEFT OF COURSE ###
items.action: Steer nothing to the right/left of the course specified.
This is a query from the Conn to ascertain the current ridder placement. The Helmsman replies, “MY RUDDER IS RIGHT/LEFT ### DEGREES.”
A command given to the Helmsman to state the heading of the ship at the moment the command was given. The Helmsman responds, “MARK ###.”
Shifting back and forth between a set number of degrees of right and left rudder as ordered by the OOD.
A command from the Conn, CO, OOD (if separate), or the Navigator to the Helmsman to pay closer attention to their steering.

coast_guard_missions.section: 11 Missions of the U.S. Coast Guard

activities: Operate a national distress/response communication system.
Operate surface and air assets.
Plan, coordinate, and conduct search and rescue operations for persons and property in distress.
Establish standards and conduct vessel inspections to ensure the safety of passengers and crew aboard commercial vessels.
Partner with states and boating safety organizations to reduce recreational boating accidents and deaths.
Investigate marine casualties.
License U.S. mariners.
Conduct harbor patrols and complete vulnerability assessments.
Enforce security zones.
Approve vessel and facility security plans; ensure compliance.
Develop Area Maritime Security Plans and conduct risk assessments.
Assess foreign port antiterrorism measures, and other activities
to prevent terrorist attacks and minimize the damage.
Deploy cutters, aircraft and deployable specialized forces to
conduct patrols, interdict and seize maritime drug trafficking vessels.
Deploy cutters and aircraft to prevent, disrupt and interdict maritime smuggling and maritime migration by
undocumentedmigrants to the U.S.
Provide forces to the Department of Defense (DoD) to perform jointmilitary operations worldwide.
Deploy cutters, boats, aircraft and deployable specialized forces in and around harbors to protect DoD force mobilization operations in the U.S. and expeditionary
operations overseas.
Conduct Polar Operations to facilitate the movement of critical goods and personnel in support of scientific requirements, nationalsecurity activities and maritime safety.
Conduct domestic icebreaking operations to facilitate navigation and commerce.
Conduct International Ice Patrol operations.

Monitorand coordinate marine traffic in keyports and waterways through Vessel Traffic Services.
Regulate construction and operation ofbridges that span navigable waters.
Prevent and respond to oil and hazardous substance spills.
Preventillegal dumping in U.S. waters.
Prevent invasions by aquatic nuisance species.
Safeguard U.S. living marineresources and their environment, toinclude protected species, protectedareas, and critical habitats, from unlawful acts and
environmental degradation.
Protect the U.S. maritime borders, EEZ, and relevant areas of the highseas by detecting, deterring, and
interdicting foreign vessels engaged in illegal activities.

items.name: Aviation Maintenance Technician
items.description: Inspects, services, maintains, troubleshoots, and repairs aircraft engines, auxiliary power units, propellers, rotor systems, power train systems, and associated airframe and systems-specific electrical components. AMTs service, maintain and repair aircraft fuselages; wings; rotor blades; fixed and movable flight control surfaces, and bleeds aircraft air, hydraulic and fuel systems.

items.name: Aviation Survival Technician
items.description: Inspects, services, maintains, troubleshoots, and repairs aircraft and aircrew survival equipment and rescue devices. Provides aircrew survival training to all aviators. ASTs deploy into a myriad of challenging rescues ranging from hurricanes and cliff rescues to emergency medical evacuations from ships at sea.

items.name: Avionics Electrical Technician
items.description: Inspects, services, maintains, troubleshoots, and repairs avionics systems that perform communications, navigation, collision avoidance, target acquisition, and automatic flight-control functions, as well as the electrical control and indication functions of all airframe systems, including hydraulics, flight control, landing gear, fuel, environmental control, power plant, drive train, anti-ice, and fire detection.

items.name: Boatswain’s Mate
items.description: Masters of seamanship and capable of performing almost any task in connection with deck maintenance, small boat operations, navigation, law enforcement, aids to navigation, and supervising all personnel assigned to a ship’s work force or small boat station. BMs are the only rating that has command of cutters and stations outside of the officer corps.

items.name: Gunner’s Mate
items.description: Operates and accounts for weapons ordnance, from 9mm small arms to shipboard 57mm and 76mm Gun Weapon Systems. Responsible for training personnel in proper handling of weapons, ammunition, and pyrotechnics. GMs receive training in electronics, mechanical systems and hydraulics to operate and maintain ordnance and gunnery equipment. GMs also have a long history of direct participation and support of Law Enforcement operations as Boarding Team Members and Boarding Officers.

items.name: Operations Specialist
items.description: Plays a central role in protecting the public from all maritime threats and hazards through command, control, and communications (C3) of boats, cutters, aircraft and personnel. They develop search and rescue plans to save mariners in distress, oversee law enforcement operations, and gather and apply intelligence information while operating the most advanced tactical computer systems in the Coast Guard.

items.name: Intelligence Specialist
items.description: Collects and interprets intelligence from raw information; analyzes communication signals and prepares graphics, overlays, and photo/map composites for mission briefs. ISs maintain intelligence databases, libraries and files.

items.name: Maritime Enforcement Specialist
items.description: Serves as law enforcement professionals in areas such as: inter-agency operations, security and response, security and anti-terrorism force protection, training, and administration.

items.name: Diver
items.description: Operates diving equipment, air supply systems, sonars, underwater power tools, and remotely operated vehicles. Divers conduct searches, recoveries, investigations, and underwater repair in various subsurface conditions from equatorial to arctic temperatures, pristine and contaminated waters, and in unlimited to zero visibility.

items.name: Damage Controlman
items.description: Responsible for ship hulls, emergency equipment, plumbing, welding, chemical biological, and radiological warfare detection, defense and decontamination, and shore side building and housing maintenance.

items.name: Electricians Mate
items.description: Tests, maintains, and repairs propulsion control systems, power distribution systems, lighting systems, motors and controllers, interior communication systems, galley, scullery, and laundry equipment, electric damage control equipment, and deck machinery equipment.

items.name: Machinery Technician
items.description: Operates, maintains, and repairs internal combustion engines, boilers, steam turbines, and main propulsion power transmission equipment; operates, maintains, and repairs auxiliary fireroom, refrigeration, air conditioning, electrical, and machine shop equipment; organizes, leads, and participates in damage control repair parties, and performs maintenance-related administrative functions.

items.name: Marine Science Technician
items.description: Facilitates commerce through waterway management and conducting inspections of marine transportation regulated facilities, intermodal containers, and foreign and domestic vessels, ensuring compliance with federal and international laws, regulations, and treaties. Contingency Planning and Emergency Management Specialists; supporting the prevention, mitigation and management of oil spills, hazardous material releases, natural and man-made disasters and enforces environmental laws and regulations.

items.name: Electronics Technician
items.description: Responsible for the installation, maintenance, repair and management of sophisticated electronic equipment, including command and control systems, shipboard weapons, communications receivers and transmitters, data and voice-encryption equipment, navigation and search radar, tactical electronic detection systems, and electronic navigation equipment.

items.name: Information Systems Technician
items.description: Responsible for establishing and maintaining Coast Guard computer systems, analog and digital voice systems (telephones and voicemail) and installing and maintaining the physical network infrastructure that ties the systems together.

items.name: Health Services Technician
items.description: Performs duties as assistant in the prevention and treatment of disease and injuries in small to large clinics. Services include direct medical care for personnel and families; assisting medical and dental officers; performing diagnostic testing, x-rays, and clinical lab tests; prescribing medications; administering immunizations; performing minor surgical procedures.

items.name: Culinary Specialist
items.description: Chefs that perform all facets of food including baking, sauces, seafood cookery, starch cookery, cake decorating and protein fabrication. Additionally, CSs perform duties of accounting and purchasing, inventory management, nutrition and preparing menus, inspecting galleys and food for safety, sanitation, and health standards.

items.name: Storekeeper
items.description: Responsible for procurements, financial transactions, shipping and receiving, as well as record keeping of general and accountable property throughout the Coast Guard.

items.name: Yeoman
items.description: Performs general clerical administrative and secretarial duties including typing, filing, records management, office publications maintenance, and office equipment operation; maintains personnel service and accounting records.

items.name: Musician
items.description: Highly skilled members that perform in the Coast Guard Band, stationed in New London, CT. Provides musical support during official ceremonies and events, including solos and ensembles. Members perform in ceremonial and concert events nationally and internationally.

items.name: Public Affairs Specialist
items.description: Supervises or participates in the administration of public affairs activities. Serves as the Coast Guard's public-communications experts, arranges and conducts interviews, writes news releases and feature articles, shoots still and video imagery, serves as spokespersons, and maintains websites to raise public awareness of important Coast Guard issues and news stories.

items.name: Cyber Mission Specialist
items.description: Plays a crucial role in operating a secure cyber space for the Service, protecting the Marine Transportation System (MTS) against malicious actors seeking to identify new ways to exploit cyber space, and countering adversaries’ intent on disrupting Coast Guard operations or negatively impacting national interests. These members will continue to serve in critical positions within CG Cyber Command, US Cyber Command, DHS Cyber Security and elsewhere when required.

items.name: Investigator
items.description: Provides support to Coast Guard law enforcement and intelligence missions. Conducts both criminal and personal background investigations, collects and analyzes intelligence information and provides personal protection services to high-ranking Coast Guard officials and other VIPs.

rotary_wing.description: Rotary-Wing Aircraft. These aircraft deploy primarily from land-based Coast Guard Air Stationsor underway cutters to conduct airborne operations supporting all Coast Guard missions. They consist of Medium Range Response (MRR) and Short-Range Response (SRR) helicopters. These aircraft conduct operations supporting all Coast Guard missions

fixed_wing.description: Fixed-Wing Aircraft. These all-weather aircraft deploy primarily from land-based Coast Guard Air Stations to conduct airborne operations. They consist of Long-Range Surveillance (LRS) andMedium Range Surveillance (MRS) aircraft. These aircraft conduct operations supporting all Coast Guard missions and perform mission support activities (e.g., logistics/transport flights)

items.title: The Coast Guard Ensign was first designed to distinguish Revenue Cutters from pirate ships. It consists of 16 alternating red and white vertical stripes, representing the number of states inthe Union when the ensign was officially adopted. The union of the Ensign contains the armsof the United States in dark blue on a white field. The Arms of the United States is an Eagle with an olive branch in one claw, and with 13 leaves and 13 arrows in the other claw. The shield on the chest of the Eagle contains 13 stripes and the circle above the Eagle contains 13stars, corresponding to the 13 original states when the nation was established. In the 1800s, the Ensign was flown from customhouses. In order to distinguish the Ensign flown on cuttersfrom the Ensign flown on customhouses, President Taft ordered that the Coast Guard emblembe added in blue and white on a line with the lower edge of the union, over the seventh vertical red stripe from the mast with a width of three stripes. (below left)

The Standard is the upper left corner of the Coast Guard Ensign which contains the arms ofthe United States. The Standard is used for parades and ceremonies, and it is adorned withthe Coast Guard battle streamers. (above right)

The Jack is the upper corner of the National Ensign nearest the mast, the blue rectangle with the 50 stars. Cutters have flown the Jack since the Civil War. The Jack is only flown from the jack staff while at anchor or at pier side.
The current Commissioning Pennant has 13 white stars on a blue field, 13 vertical red-and-white stripes, and a red swallowtail. This pennant is flown from the top of the mainmast.

items.text: Conditions of Material Readiness
X - Ray: Provides the least protection. Set when the ship is in no danger of attack. A black X isplaced on all fittings that shall be closed at all times when not in operation.

Yoke: Set and maintained at sea and in port during wartime. For peacetime cruising, Yoke may be modified during regular working hours. A black Y is placed on all fittings that shall beclosed for wartime cruising conditions.

Zebra: Provides the maximum protection for ship and personnel for battle and emergency situations, such as fire, collision, or General Quarters, and is set when entering or leaving portduring wartime. A Z is placed on all fittings that shall be closed for battle or emergency conditions.
Special Classification
Circle Williams: This is classified by a black “W” within a black circle. The fittings are closed only to prevent the spread of Chemical/Biological/Radiological (CBR) contaminationor for defense.
Dog Zebra: This classification is indicated by a red Z enclosed by a large black D. It is placedon fittings that must be secured to prevent light escaping outside the ship.
Fire Tetrahedron

The fire tetrahedron refers to the four components that are needed for a fire to occur and maintain itself: heat, oxygen, fuel, and chain reaction. When you eliminate any or all of these components, you no longer have a fire tetrahedron and the fire should be extinguished.
Class A fires involve wood and wood products, cloth, textiles and fibrous materials, and paper products.

Class A fires are extinguished with water in a straight stream or fog pattern. If the fire is deep-seated, Aqueous Film Forming Foam (AFFF) is more effective than seawater and can be used as a wetting agent to rapidly penetrate and extinguish the fire.
Class B fires involve flammable liquids such as gasoline, diesel fuel, jet fuels, hydraulic fluid, and lube oil.

These fires are normally extinguished with AFFF, or potassium bicarbonate (PKP). Class B fires also involve flammable gases which should neverbe extinguished unless there is reasonable certainty that the flow of gas can be secured. Securing the fuel source is the single most important step in controlling a gas fire.
Class C fires are energized electrical fires.

They are attacked at prescribed distances using nonconductive agents such as CO2 or water spray. The most effective tactic is tode-energize and handle the fire as a Class A fire. When fires are not deep seated, clean agentsthat pose no cleanup problem such as CO2 are preferred.
Class D fires involve combustible metals such as magnesium and titanium.

Water in quantity,using fog patterns, is the recommended agent. When water is applied to bufrom a safe distance or from behind shelter. Metal fires on board ships are commonly associated with aircraft wheel structures. If the fire cannot be contained, jettison the object overboard.
Academy and Military Etiquette
Addressing Officers, Upper-class, and Civilians

Show the proper respect in all relations with officers, upper-class, and civilians. The word “Sir” or “Ma’am” is always used by a junior to a senior. This is not a term of submission, butof respect that should be used at all times.

When addressing a senior, say “Mister” or “Miss” Last Name, except when the senior’s rank is Commander (O-5) and above, in which case the rank is substitutedfor “Mister” or “Miss.” For example, “Good morning CDR Johnson, ma’am” or “Good evening CAPT Ray, sir.”
When addressing a group of officers, greet only the highest-ranking officer.
If you are covered, render a salute and hold it until all of the officers acknowledge orpass by you.

If you wish to pass an officer or an upper-class cadet in the barracks, you are to obtainpermission by asking “By your leave please, Sir/Ma’am?” If you are covered, render asalute to officers both indoors and outdoors.
Handshakes shall only be initiated by the senior person.

The Academy operates on a four-class system. The use of first names is permitted betweenadjoining upper-class (not 4/c) only in informal settings. During official business, a junior cadet shall not use the first name of a cadet from a more senior class.
Entering or Leaving a Superior’s Room or Office
Whenever entering an officer’s/civilian’s office or an upper-class’s room, adhere to thefollowing guidelines:
Knock.
Loudly state your name and state your business. For example, “4/c, request permission to come aboard Sir/Ma’am.”

When on duty or at any time under arms or wearing a drill belt, you will remain covered, except in the wardroom, mess hall, or place of worship. When on duty, announce your presence with “4/c , Bravo Company Orderly, requests permission to come aboard, Sir/Ma’am.” When covered, salute upon entering andexiting an officer’s office.
When asking to leave a civilian or officer’s office or an upper-class’s room ask,“By your leave, Sir/Ma’am?”
On being excused, turn around and leave, DO NOT about face.

Quarterdeck Customs
Do not be loud or sloppy in its vicinity.
Never appear on the quarterdeck unless wearing the UOD or member of a work party.
Never smoke on the quarterdeck.
Never cross or walk on the quarterdeck except when necessary.
Do not lounge in the vicinity of the quarterdeck.
Sickbay Customs
Always remove your cover when entering sickbay out of respect for the dead. Maintain quiet atall times and do not smoke in sickbay.
Messdeck Customs

Always remove your cover when entering the sickbay, the mess deck, or the wardroom. Never leave your cover on the table, as to respect the men and women that lost their lives on mess decktables in times of war.
Bridge Customs

When a member is on the bridge and the Commanding Officer (CO) arrives, the member will call: 'Captain on the Bridge' and salute the CO. Upon the CO departing, the member will call: 'Captain Below' and salute the CO as they leave. All members are responsible to uphold this standard. This protocol is to show respect and can be dispensed of at the CO’s discretion.
Divine Services

The ship flies the church pennant above the national ensign when divine services are being held.An announcement is made informing the ship where services will be held. Always remove yourcover in the area of divine services and remain quiet about the decks.
Whom to salute:
All commissioned and warrant officers of the Coast Guard, Navy, Marine Corps, Air Force, and Army.
Officers of foreign armed services unless we are at war with them.
Officers of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the Public HealthServices (USPHS).
If an officer is recognized in civilian attire, a salute shall still be rendered.
When to salute:
Six paces away is the general rule, but salute and greet at the same time you would if you were greeting a civilian.
Always accompany your salute with a cheerful, respectful greeting.

When transiting with a commissioned officer: Do not salute another officer until the officer with you salutes- then salute at the same time your officer does. If you are accompanying acommissioned officer who is saluted by an enlisted member or another cadet, return the salute at the same time your officer does.
When conversing with an officer: salute when approaching the officer, then salute the officer again at the end of the conversation.
When on Duty:
As a cadet, you stand a variety of duties including “Comp Chomp” during Fourth Class year, and on this duty, you remain covered inside.
If approached by an officer while on duty and covered, render the proper salute to them whether or not they are covered as well.
The Coast Guardsman’s Manual Ch 21: Communications
Parts of a Message: To whom, from whom, about what (the name of the person/thing being called, the name of the person/thing calling, and the information to be sent). “To who, From who, About what”
Circuit Discipline: To prevent confusion, strict circuit discipline must be maintained.
Send only official messages
Keep button in the off position except when actually talking
Use only standard phraseology
Never show anger, impatience, or excitement Transmitting Techniques: The following techniques will ensure good communication:
Listen before transmitting
Do not break in on a message
Speak clearly, distinctly, and slowly, but transmit phrase by phrase, not word by word
Use standard pronunciation, use standard terminology, and always use prescribed procedures
Procedure Words: Procedure words (prowords) are words and phrases used to speed up radio communication.
